questions.prompt: In Anthropic's "Building effective agents" post, what makes a system an agent rather than a workflow?

options.text: It uses the largest model the vendor offers.
options.explanation: The post's split is about who decides the steps, not model size.

options.text: The model directs its own process and chooses which tools to use.
options.explanation: Right. In a workflow the path is set in advance; an agent decides how to do the task.

options.text: It talks to customers instead of staff.
options.explanation: Who it talks to doesn't matter. The post looks at who controls the steps.

questions.prompt: Both Anthropic's and OpenAI's docs describe the same basic agent loop. Which one?

options.text: Call the model, run any tool calls, feed the results back, repeat until there is a final answer.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's Agent SDK docs and OpenAI's running-agents guide both describe this loop.

options.text: Write one answer, send it to a person, and wait for the next day's batch.
options.explanation: That is a single call with human review, not a loop with tools.

options.text: Train the model on your data each night, then answer questions the next morning.
options.explanation: The loop happens at run time with tools. Neither page describes nightly training.

questions.prompt: According to Anthropic's post, what is usually enough for many applications?

options.text: A team of several agents that check each other's work.
options.explanation: The post recommends the simplest solution, and adds complexity only when needed.

options.text: An agent with no limits, so it can finish any task.
options.explanation: The post warns that agents bring higher costs and compounding errors.

options.text: One well-built model call with retrieval and in-context examples.
options.explanation: Right. The post says this is usually enough, and an agentic system may not be needed at all.
